# Leviticus 1: Research notes

**Coverage:** The Enduring Word page loaded only through v. 5. For vv. 9 and 14–17 I used its summary in the search results. I found no Orthodox source (oca.org), nothing on bibleodyssey.org, and no prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. I also didn't find any real split between Protestant denominations here. What I did find are a few debates about what the offering means, listed in Part 2.

## Part 1: Verse by verse

**v. 1**
- Guzik: Israel is still at Sinai. Speaking "from the tabernacle" means the tabernacle is finished, so the sacrifices can now begin. He links it to John 1:14, where the Word "tabernacled" among us. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-1/
- NET note: the opening "He called" ties back to Exodus 40:35. Moses couldn't go into the tent because the glory cloud filled it, so the LORD called to him from inside. "Tent of meeting" names it as the place where God and people meet. "Tabernacle" names it as God's home. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=lev+1&6%3A8-13=&mode=print

**v. 2**
- Guzik: Only tame herd or flock animals could be offered, never wild ones. These animals were part of a family's living, so a sacrifice cost something. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-1/
- NET note: The Hebrew word behind "any of you" (*adam*) means any person, man or woman. Women also brought offerings (Lev 12:6–8). Vv. 1–2 introduce all of chapters 1–3. Birds aren't mentioned here because bird offerings were mostly an allowance for the poor. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=lev+1&6%3A8-13=&mode=print

**v. 3**
- Pulpit Commentary: the burnt offering was the first two [parts] to be performed by the offerer, the third by the priest, the fourth by the fire representing the action of God. The moral lesson taught by the burnt offering was the necessity of self-surrender. Its fulfilment is Christ's perfect surrender, above all in Gethsemane and on the cross. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/1-3.htm
- Guzik: Male animals were seen as stronger and more valuable. "Without blemish" points to Christ, the spotless sacrifice (1 Peter 1:19). God deserves our best (Malachi 1:8). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-1/
- Matthew Henry: The animal was offered at the door, as one unworthy to enter, and acknowledging that there is no admission for a sinner into covenant and communion with God, but by sacrifice. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_001.cfm
- Wesley: The door shows that no one can enter the church or heaven except through Christ, who is the door (John 10:7, 9). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/1.htm
- NET note: "For its acceptance" most likely means the animal was being accepted on the worshipper's behalf. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=lev+1&6%3A8-13=&mode=print

**v. 4**
- Pulpit Commentary: The offerer pressed or leaned his hand on the animal's head. This said, in effect, "this animal now stands for me." The sin offering is the main atoning sacrifice, but the idea of atonement is not absent from the burnt sacrifice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/1-4.htm
- Gill: The hand-laying meant sins were passed to the animal, a picture of our sins being counted to Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/1-4.htm
- Guzik: Atonement means "to cover." In the Old Testament sin was covered until Jesus dealt with it fully. Laying on hands may have come with confession of sin (compare Lev 16:21). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-1/
- Maclaren: Nothing is said of confession here; but we cannot dismiss the idea that the offerer laid his sins on the victim. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/leviticus/burnt-offering.cfm
- Matthew Henry: Burnt offerings didn't deal with one particular sin, but they did make atonement for sin in general. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_001.cfm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: The person who laid his hand on the animal seems to have killed it himself. That act admitted, "I need atonement for my sin." The phrase "before the LORD" appears more than 60 times in Leviticus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-1/
- NET note: The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) says "they" killed it, which suggests the priests did. The word usually translated "sprinkle" really means "splash" or "dash." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=lev+1&6%3A8-13=&mode=print
- Wesley: The splashed blood showed that the offerer deserved to die, and that Christ's blood is the only way to be reconciled to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/1.htm

**v. 6**
- Matthew Poole gives two reasons for skinning:
  - It was fitting, since God shouldn't be given what people wouldn't eat.
  - It showed that God looks at the inside of a person.

  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/1-6.htm
- Gill: The skinning pictures Christ's sufferings. The skin, which went to the priest, pictures Christ's righteousness given to believers. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/1-6.htm
- NET note: Some ancient versions say the priests did the skinning. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=lev+1&6%3A8-13=&mode=print

**v. 7**
- Wesley: The altar fire came down from heaven (Lev 9:24) and had to be kept burning. Any other fire was forbidden. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/1.htm
- NET note: The Hebrew has "priest" singular here. Several ancient versions have "priests." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=lev+1&6%3A8-13=&mode=print

**v. 8**
- NET note: "Fat" here means suet, the hard fat around the kidneys. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=lev+1&6%3A8-13=&mode=print
- Wesley: The fat was laid on to make the fire burn hotter. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/1.htm

**v. 9**
- Wesley: Washing the insides and legs pictures purity of heart and of conduct, perfect in Christ and to be sought by Christians. The smell was sweet not in itself but because it pictured Christ's offering of himself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/1.htm
- Poole and Trapp (quoted by Guzik): burning flesh actually "rather caused a stink". https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-1/
- Pulpit Commentary: "Sweet savour" is used of the burnt, grain and peace offerings, never of the sin or guilt offerings. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-1.html
- Clarke: Paul had this phrase in mind in Ephesians 5:2. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/1-9.html
- Precept Austin: The fire itself wasn't the offering. It was how the offering rose to God as smoke. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_1_commentary
- NET note: The word usually rendered "offering made by fire" (*isheh*) is better translated "gift." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=lev+1&6%3A8-13=&mode=print

**v. 10**
- Wenham (quoted by Precept Austin): Only burnt and guilt offerings had to be male, and no blemish at all was allowed. This shows how highly ranked these offerings were. https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_1_commentary
- Matthew Henry: Sheep and goats were for people of middle means. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_001.cfm

**v. 11**
- Matthew Henry: The north side probably applied to the other sacrifices too. Perhaps there was more open space there. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_001.cfm

**vv. 12–13**
- NET: The offerer cuts up and washes the animal, and the priest does the burning. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=lev+1&6%3A8-13=&mode=print
- Coffman: The worshipper kept nothing for himself. The offering admitted God's full authority and promised obedience. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/1-13.html

**v. 14**
- Pulpit Commentary: Comparing Lev 12:8 shows that birds were an allowance for the poor. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-1.html
- Matthew Henry: God, in his law and in his gospel, as well as in his providence, considers the poor. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Lev/Lev_001.cfm
- Guzik: God accepted a poor person's bird as readily as a rich person's bull. But the gift had to match what you could afford, so a rich man offering only a bird was wrong. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-1/
- Wesley: Doves picture Christ's purity and gentleness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/1.htm

**v. 15**
- Wesley: The head was taken off completely. Lev 5:8, where it is not severed, is about the sin offering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/1.htm
- NET translates the verb "pinch off." https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=lev+1&6%3A8-13=&mode=print

**v. 16**
- Poole: The east side was the furthest point from the holy of holies. It teaches that unclean things can't approach God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/1-16.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: East was also nearest the courtyard entrance, so the waste could easily be carried out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/1-16.htm
- Barnes: The ashes were piled east of the altar and later carried outside the camp. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/1-16.html
- Coffman: He rejects Rashi's view that the crop was thrown away because "birds feed on what is stolen." The real reason is that it held filth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/1-16.html
- Translation: The NLT notes that the meaning of the Hebrew is uncertain. NET reads "entrails… tail feathers." https://www.blueletterbible.org/nlt/lev/1/1/s_91001

**v. 17**
- Wesley: The bird was split along its whole length but kept in one piece. He adds that loving God and neighbour is better than all burnt - offerings and sacrifices. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/1.htm
- Keil and Delitzsch: The burnt offering stands for the whole person given up to the Lord. Choosing male animals pictures a vigorous self-surrender. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/1-17.htm

## Part 2: Where interpreters differ

These are differences between particular teachers, not clear-cut denominational camps.

- **v. 4: Is this offering mainly about atonement or about dedication?**
  - Barnes: "atonement" is rarely [used] in reference to the burnt-offerings.
  - Jamieson-Fausset-Brown: it was meant to turn away God's anger over original sin or particular sins. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/leviticus/1-3.htm
  - Guzik: it is "more about total surrender… than about sin." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-1/
- **v. 4: Does laying on hands transfer guilt here?**
  - Gill and Guzik say yes.
  - Chuck Smith says hand-laying transfers guilt in the sin offering, but in the burnt offering it means the animal "taking my place" as an act of dedication. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/1-13.html
- **v. 9: Does the fire stand for God's wrath?**
  - One Precept Austin source says Christ was consumed "by the judicial wrath of God." https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_1_commentary
  - Gill says Christ's soul "felt the fire of divine wrath." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/leviticus/1-9.html
  - **Lutheran (LCMS):** a devotion says the burning did not mean God was consuming the offering in wrath. Rather, he was graciously receiving it in the offerer's place. It sees the burnt offering as about sanctification, coming after forgiveness. https://in.lcms.org/christ-our-holocaust-sacrifice/
- **v. 4: Methodist (John Wesley):** the offering made atonement "sacramentally," pointing the worshipper's faith to the true sacrifice still to come. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/leviticus/1.htm
- **Christ as burnt offering: offered to God, or for the sinner?** William Kelly and a sermon on Bible Hub say this offering shows Christ's devotion offered to God. One sermon says it is not for the sinner's conscience, but for the heart of God. https://biblehub.com/sermons/leviticus/1-3.htm

## Part 3: Other views

**Modern scholarship (NET notes)**
- v. 4: The basic meaning of *kipper* ("make atonement") is "to wipe," as in purging. It can also mean to appease someone with a gift. https://classic.net.bible.org/passage.php?passage=lev+1&6%3A8-13=&mode=print
- vv. 5–6: The Septuagint has the priests doing the killing and skinning.
- v. 9: *isheh* means "gift."
- The burnt offering could serve several purposes: fulfilling a vow, a freewill gift, going with prayer, part of the daily and festival offerings, or atonement. (same URL)

**Catholic**
- The Catholic Encyclopedia lists three purposes for the "holocaust" (whole burnt offering):
  - It recalled God's rule over all creatures and called for complete self-surrender.
  - It assured worshippers who came with the right attitude that God accepted it as atonement (v. 4).
  - It foreshadowed Christ's sacrifice.

  It rejects the critics' view that the prophets condemned sacrifice itself. They were attacking abuses of it. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/07396b.htm
- Catholic Answers: the holocaust symbolizes recognition of God's sovereignty over everything. It says only priests performed it, which differs from v. 5's offerer-led slaughter. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/leviticus
- v. 4 in the Douay-Rheims reads "help to its expiation." https://biblehub.com/leviticus/1-4.htm

**Orthodox, Bible Odyssey, prosperity / word of faith / hyper-grace:** nothing found.
